text: Policy, standard, and procedure get treated as interchangeable words for "a security document," and that habit causes real problems. This lesson draws a hard line between all three, and walks through what actually breaks when an organization writes one at the wrong level of detail.

A policy states the what and why, at a level of abstraction that survives a change of vendor or tech stack — approved by executives, sometimes the board, and changed rarely because a change is a governance event. A standard translates that into specific, measurable requirements an auditor can actually test — owned by security leadership, and changed more often. A procedure is the literal step-by-step how-to for meeting a standard, owned by the team executing it, and changed the most often of the three.

Walk the same requirement down all three levels. The policy says privileged access must use multi-factor authentication — no vendor named. The standard gets specific: a FIDO2 hardware token or authenticator app, no SMS, a 15-minute session timeout. The procedure gets literal: open the identity provider console, find the user's MFA settings, add the method, have them register their token within ten minutes.

Conflate those levels and governance breaks down in predictable ways. A policy written with procedure-level detail goes stale the moment the organization switches identity providers, and because fixing it requires executive re-approval, that staleness often just gets ignored. A standard written with policy-level vagueness, like 'use strong authentication,' can't be audited — compliance becomes a judgment call instead of a measurement. And a procedure written at policy-level abstraction leaves the executing team to improvise, so two people doing 'the same' task produce two different outcomes.
That hierarchy is also what GRC tooling is built to track — which is exactly where Lesson 3 picks up: what these tools genuinely automate, and what they were never designed to decide for you.
